topics.title: Meaning and Scope of AS 2
explain: Inventories are assets held for sale in the ordinary course of business, in the process of production, or for consumption in production of goods or services.
They include merchandise of a retailer, raw materials, WIP, finished goods, maintenance supplies, and loose tools.
Machinery spares, servicing equipment, and standby equipment meeting Property, Plant and Equipment definition fall under AS 10 (Revised), not AS 2.
AS 2 specifically excludes construction WIP covered by AS 7, though construction materials lying at site like cement are included in AS 2.
WIP of service providers (like voyage-in-progress or consulting services) and shares, debentures, or financial instruments held as stock-in-trade are excluded.
Inventories of livestock, agricultural products, mineral oils, ores, and gases measured at net realisable value under trade practices are also excluded.

flow.title: Scope Determination under AS 2
steps: Identify the asset held by the business
Check if it meets inventory definition
Verify if it is covered by AS 10
Check specific exclusions under AS 2
Apply AS 2 if not excluded

topics.example: A real estate developer holding cement at the building site values that cement under AS 2, but the half-built apartments are valued under AS 7.
remember: Cement at a construction site is governed by AS 2, not AS 7.
mistakes: Assuming all items at a construction site fall under AS 7; unused materials at site are covered by AS 2.

quiz.q: Which of the following items is covered within the scope of AS 2 (Revised)?
o: Work in progress of a software consulting firm
quiz.why: Raw materials held for production are standard inventory covered under AS 2, whereas construction WIP, shares as stock-in-trade, and service WIP are excluded.

quiz.q: How should standby equipment and machinery spares meeting the definition of PPE be accounted for?
o: Charged fully to P&L upon acquisition
quiz.why: Spares and standby equipment meeting the definition of Property, Plant and Equipment must be accounted for under AS 10 (Revised).

topics.title: Measurement Principle and Net Realisable Value (NRV)
explain: Inventories must be valued at the lower of historical cost and net realisable value (NRV).
This rule is grounded in the prudence concept, ensuring assets are not carried above what they can realise.
Net Realisable Value is the estimated selling price in the ordinary course of business minus estimated completion costs and estimated costs to make the sale.
If estimated NRV is below cost, inventory is written down and the loss is recognized in the Profit and Loss statement immediately.
If NRV exceeds cost, the anticipated gain is ignored, and inventory stays strictly at cost.

flow.title: Valuation at Lower of Cost or NRV
steps: Determine the historical cost of inventory
Calculate estimated selling price
Deduct completion and selling expenses for NRV
Compare cost with computed NRV
Value inventory at the lower figure

topics.example: An unfinished unit has cost ₹150. It needs ₹100 to complete and can sell for ₹250 with ₹10 brokerage. NRV is ₹140 (250 - 100 - 10). The unit is valued at ₹140.
remember: NRV = Estimated Selling Price - Estimated Cost of Completion - Estimated Selling Expenses.
mistakes: Forgetting to deduct selling expenses or brokerage from selling price when calculating NRV.

quiz.q: Inventory cost is ₹50,000, estimated selling price is ₹55,000, and selling commission is ₹8,000. What is the inventory value?
quiz.why: NRV is ₹55,000 - ₹8,000 = ₹47,000. Inventory is valued at the lower of cost (₹50,000) and NRV (₹47,000), which is ₹47,000.

quiz.q: The principle of valuing inventory at the lower of cost and NRV is based on which accounting concept?
quiz.why: The prudence principle demands anticipating no profits while recognizing all foreseeable losses immediately.

topics.title: Costs of Purchase and Costs of Conversion
explain: Cost of purchase includes purchase price, import duties, non-recoverable taxes, and transport costs directly attributable to acquisition.
Trade discounts, rebates, and duty drawbacks must always be deducted to find the purchase cost.
Costs of conversion include direct labor and systematic allocation of fixed and variable production overheads.
Fixed production overheads are absorbed based on normal operating capacity, not idle or low actual production.
Unabsorbed fixed overheads due to low production are expensed in P&L, never added to inventory cost.
If actual production is abnormally high, fixed overhead per unit is decreased so inventory is not carried above actual cost.

flow.title: Fixed Production Overhead Absorption
steps: Determine budgeted fixed overheads and normal capacity
Calculate standard fixed overhead absorption rate
Check actual production versus normal capacity
If production is normal or low, use standard rate
Expense unabsorbed overhead directly to P&L
If production is abnormally high, recompute actual lower rate

topics.example: Fixed overheads are ₹18 lakhs and normal capacity is 1,00,000 units (₹18/unit). If only 90,000 units are made, inventory absorbs ₹18/unit (₹16.2 lakhs) and ₹1.8 lakhs goes directly to P&L.
remember: Low production never increases the fixed overhead rate per unit; high production lowers it to avoid over-costing.
mistakes: Dividing fixed overheads by actual low production, which artificially inflates inventory value and hides period losses.

quiz.q: Fixed overhead is ₹20 lakhs and normal capacity is 2,00,000 units. Actual production is 1,60,000 units. How much fixed overhead is included in closing inventory of 10,000 units?
quiz.why: Rate based on normal capacity is ₹20,00,000 / 2,00,000 = ₹10 per unit. Inventory absorbs 10,000 units × ₹10 = ₹1,00,000.

quiz.q: When actual production is abnormally higher than normal capacity, how are fixed overheads allocated?
o: At the normal capacity rate, creating an over-recovery reserve
At a decreased actual rate so inventories are not valued above cost
Ignored completely from cost of conversion
quiz.why: In abnormally high production, the rate per unit is decreased using actual production to ensure inventories are not measured above actual cost.

topics.title: Joint Products and By-Products
explain: When a production process yields more than one product together, common joint costs must be allocated rationally up to the split-off point.
Allocation is typically done on the relative sales value of the products at split-off or at completion of production.
By-products, scrap, and industrial waste have minor value and are not assigned separate joint costs.
By-products and scrap are measured at their net realisable value.
The NRV of by-products is deducted from the total joint production cost, leaving the balance as the cost of the main product.

flow.title: Costing of Joint and By-Products
steps: Accumulate total production costs to split-off
Identify main joint products and minor by-products
Calculate net realisable value of by-products
Deduct by-product NRV from total joint cost
Allocate remaining cost among main products by sales value

topics.example: Refining crude oil produces petrol and diesel (joint products) plus minor bitumen residue (by-product). Bitumen's NRV is deducted from refining costs before splitting costs between petrol and diesel.
remember: Cost of Main Product = Total Joint Cost - NRV of By-products/Scraps.
mistakes: Treating by-products like main joint products by allocating full overheads to them instead of merely deducting their NRV.

quiz.q: How are by-products of immaterial value accounted for under AS 2?
o: Allocated joint costs based on output weight
Valued at NRV, which is deducted from main product cost
Valued at historical cost plus standard mark-up
quiz.why: By-products are measured at net realisable value and this value is deducted from the total joint cost of the main product.

quiz.q: Joint costs incurred up to the split-off point are most commonly allocated on the basis of:
o: Relative sales value at split-off or completion
Equal division among all outputs regardless of value
quiz.why: AS 2 states allocation may be based on the relative sale value of each product either at the split-off stage or at completion.

topics.title: Other Costs and Exclusions from Inventory
explain: Other costs are included in inventory only if incurred to bring inventories to their present location and condition (e.g., custom design costs).
Interest and borrowing costs are generally excluded unless the inventory necessarily takes a substantial period to get ready for sale (e.g., maturing wine).
Amortisation of production-related intangibles (like manufacturing patents or copyright) forms part of inventory cost.
Foreign exchange differences are strictly excluded from inventory costs.
Abnormal amounts of wasted materials, idle labor, or other production inefficiencies must be expensed in P&L.
Storage costs are excluded unless storage is an essential step in the production process prior to a further stage.
Administrative overheads that do not contribute to bringing inventory to its present location and condition, plus all selling and distribution costs, are excluded.

flow.title: Testing Costs for Inclusion or Exclusion
steps: Check if cost brings inventory to present location and condition
If selling, distribution, or general admin cost, exclude immediately
If abnormal wastage or unnecessary storage, expense in P&L
If borrowing cost, include only for qualifying maturing inventory
Include valid custom design and production intangibles in cost

topics.example: In a winery, storage costs during the natural aging process of wine are included in cost, whereas storage of finished bottled wine in a retail warehouse is excluded.
remember: Abnormal waste, general admin, storage of finished goods, and selling costs are NEVER part of inventory cost.
mistakes: Capitalizing storage costs of finished goods waiting to be sold into inventory valuation.

quiz.q: Which of the following costs is included in the cost of inventory under AS 2?
o: Cost of designing products for a specific custom order
Storage costs of finished goods awaiting delivery
quiz.why: Costs of design for a custom-made unit are incurred to bring the inventory to its present condition and are included.

quiz.q: When can borrowing costs be added to the cost of inventory?
o: Whenever funds are borrowed to purchase raw materials
Only when inventory takes a substantial period to get ready for intended sale
Whenever management chooses under accounting policy
Borrowing costs can never be included under any circumstance
quiz.why: Borrowing costs are included only where inventory necessarily takes a substantial period of time to get ready for sale, such as maturing wine.

topics.title: Cost Formulas and Cost Measurement Techniques
explain: Specific Identification method is mandatory for items that are not ordinarily interchangeable or goods segregated for specific projects.
When specific identification is not practicable, inventory cost must be determined using First-In First-Out (FIFO) or Weighted Average Cost formula.
The formula chosen should provide the fairest approximation to the cost incurred in bringing goods to their present location and condition.
Standard Costing may be used for convenience if standards approximate actual costs and are regularly reviewed and updated.
Retail Method (Adjusted Selling Price method) is used in retail businesses with large volumes of rapidly changing items with similar margins.
Under the Retail Method, cost is computed by taking the total retail sales value of unsold stock and deducting the appropriate percentage of gross margin.

flow.title: Selecting the Right Cost Formula
steps: Are items segregated for specific projects?
If yes, apply Specific Identification method
If no, choose between FIFO or Weighted Average
For high-volume retail trades, use Retail Method
Deduct gross margin percentage from retail sales value

topics.example: A clothing store has unsold clothes with a retail price of ₹20,000 and standard markup is 25% on cost (margin of 20% on retail). Cost of unsold stock = ₹20,000 - (₹20,000 / 1.25 × 0.25) = ₹16,000.
remember: Mark-up is calculated on cost; margin is calculated on selling price.
mistakes: Confusing 25% mark-up on cost with 25% margin on sales when computing retail stock value.

quiz.q: Which cost formula is compulsory for items produced and segregated for specific unique customer projects?
quiz.why: AS 2 requires specific identification of costs for items not ordinarily interchangeable and goods produced for specific projects.

quiz.q: A retailer has unsold stock with a sale value of ₹1,00,000. The business operates on a 25% gross margin on sales. What is the inventory cost?
quiz.why: Cost = Sale value - Gross margin = ₹1,00,000 - (25% of ₹1,00,000) = ₹75,000.

topics.title: Item-by-Item Valuation and Materials Held for Production
explain: Comparison of cost and NRV should be made on an item-by-item basis rather than on a global or whole-portfolio basis.
Raw materials and supplies held for use in production are NOT written down below cost if the finished products will be sold at or above cost.
If finished goods are expected to sell at or above cost, the raw materials are deemed to realize their cost.
However, if finished product price falls such that finished product cost exceeds its NRV, raw materials are written down.
In that case, the replacement cost of the raw material is taken as the best available measure of its net realisable value.
Partly finished goods (WIP) are valued at lower of cost incurred and estimated selling price of finished goods less further completion and selling costs.

flow.title: Raw Material Valuation Decision
steps: Check expected selling price of finished good
Compare finished good price against its total cost
If finished good sells at or above cost, keep raw material at cost
If finished good sells below cost, write down raw material
Value raw material at its current replacement cost

topics.example: Raw material was purchased for ₹120, replacement cost is ₹90. Total cost of finished product is ₹320 but selling price drops to ₹300. Because the finished product sells at a loss, raw material is written down to its replacement cost of ₹90.
remember: Raw materials are written down to replacement cost ONLY IF the related finished goods are sold below cost.
mistakes: Automatically writing down raw materials to replacement cost just because replacement cost fell, without checking whether the finished product sells at a profit.

quiz.q: Raw material cost is ₹100 and its replacement cost is ₹80. The finished good made from it costs ₹250 and sells for ₹270. At what value should raw material be carried?
quiz.why: Because the finished good is sold at ₹270 (above its cost of ₹250), raw materials are not written down and remain at cost of ₹100.

quiz.q: When calculating closing inventory containing items A, B, and C, how should the lower of cost and NRV rule be applied?
o: By comparing total portfolio cost against total portfolio NRV
By averaging the costs and NRVs across all products
At the discretion of company management
quiz.why: AS 2 mandates that comparison of cost and net realisable value should normally be made on an item-by-item basis.

topics.title: Disclosures in Financial Statements
explain: Financial statements must disclose the accounting policies adopted in measuring inventories, including the specific cost formula used (FIFO, Weighted Average, etc.).
The total carrying amount of inventories must be disclosed along with appropriate classifications.
Standard classifications include raw materials and components, work-in-progress, finished goods, stock-in-trade (goods purchased for resale), stores and spares, loose tools, and others.
Net realisable value must be assessed and reviewed at each balance sheet date.
Part I of Schedule III to the Companies Act, 2013 also requires companies to disclose the valuation mode of each class of inventories.

flow.title: Inventory Reporting and Disclosure Checklist
steps: State accounting policy adopted for inventory
Disclose specific cost formulas used
Classify inventory into raw materials, WIP, and finished goods
Include stores, spares, loose tools, and stock-in-trade
Report total carrying amount as per Schedule III

topics.example: A company notes in its balance sheet: 'Inventories are valued at lower of cost (determined using FIFO formula) and net realisable value' and breaks down the balance into raw materials, WIP, and finished goods.
remember: Both the measurement policy AND the cost formula used must be explicitly disclosed.
mistakes: Disclosing just 'inventories are at lower of cost and NRV' while omitting the specific cost formula (e.g., FIFO or WAM) used.

quiz.q: Which of the following disclosures is required by AS 2 (Revised)?
o: Names of all suppliers from whom raw materials were bought
Accounting policies and cost formula adopted for inventory measurement
Estimated profit margin on every unsold inventory item
Forecast of next year's raw material purchase prices
quiz.why: The financial statements must disclose accounting policies adopted, including the cost formula used, and total carrying amount by classification.

quiz.q: Which statutory schedule under the Companies Act, 2013 mandates disclosure of the inventory valuation mode?
quiz.why: Part I of Schedule III to the Companies Act, 2013 prescribes that the valuation method should be disclosed for inventory held by companies.
